name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q01 - Minimum frequency to dissociate carbon monoxide molecule

questiontext.text: 8.1 One requires \(11\text{ eV}\) of energy to dissociate a carbon monoxide molecule into carbon and oxygen atoms. The minimum frequency of the appropriate electromagnetic radiation to achieve the dissociation lies in

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The dissociation energy required for a carbon monoxide molecule is \(E = 11 ext{ eV}\). The elementary charge is \(e = 1.6 imes 10^{-19} ext{ C}\), and Planck's constant is \(h = 6.626 imes 10^{-34} ext{ J s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A single photon of electromagnetic radiation supplies the minimum energy required for dissociation, so the photon energy equals the dissociation energy.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The energy of a photon of frequency \( u\) is given by Planck's relation: \[E = h u \implies u = rac{E}{h}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Converting the energy from electron-volts to joules: \[E = 11 imes 1.6 imes 10^{-19} ext{ J} = 1.76 imes 10^{-18} ext{ J}\] Substituting into the frequency formula: \[ u = rac{1.76 imes 10^{-18} ext{ J}}{6.626 imes 10^{-34} ext{ J s}} \approx 2.66 imes 10^{15} ext{ Hz}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The frequency \(2.66 imes 10^{15} ext{ Hz}\) (corresponding to a wavelength of about \(113 ext{ nm}\)) is higher than the visible spectrum (\(4 imes 10^{14} ext{ Hz}\) to \(7.5 imes 10^{14} ext{ Hz}\)) and lies well within the ultraviolet range (\(7.5 imes 10^{14} ext{ Hz}\) to \(3 imes 10^{16} ext{ Hz}\)). Therefore, the minimum frequency lies in the ultraviolet region.

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q02 - Reflected linearly polarized wave from infinite wall

questiontext.text: 8.2 A linearly polarized electromagnetic wave given as \(\mathbf{E} = E_0\hat{\mathbf{i}}\cos(kz - \omega t)\) is incident normally on a perfectly reflecting infinite wall at \(z = a\). Assuming that the material of the wall is optically inactive, the reflected wave will be given as

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The incident linearly polarized electromagnetic wave is \(\mathbf{E} = E_0\hat{\mathbf{i}}\cos(kz - \omega t)\), propagating along the \(+z\)-direction, incident normally on a perfectly reflecting, optically inactive infinite wall at \(z = a\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The incident wave travels in the \(+z\)-direction, so the reflected wave travels in the \(-z\)-direction. Because the wall is optically inactive, the plane of polarization does not rotate. Upon reflection from a perfectly reflecting (rigid/denser) boundary, the electric field undergoes a phase change of \(\pi\text{ rad}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Reversing the propagation direction from \(+z\) to \(-z\) replaces \(kz - \omega t\) with \(kz + \omega t\) (up to a constant phase shift from the boundary position). A phase change of \(\pi\) introduces a factor of \(\cos(\theta + \pi) = -\cos(\theta)\), reversing the electric field vector.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
1. Reversing the direction of propagation changes the phase argument from \((kz - \omega t)\) to \((kz + \omega t)\).
2. Applying the \(\pi\) phase shift on reflection reverses the sign of the electric field amplitude from \(+E_0\hat{\mathbf{i}}\) to \(-E_0\hat{\mathbf{i}}\).
3. Combining these gives the reflected electric field: \[\mathbf{E}_r = -E_0\hat{\mathbf{i}}\cos(kz + \omega t)\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The wave travels in the \(-z\)-direction (since \(kz + \omega t = \text{constant} \implies \frac{dz}{dt} = -\frac{\omega}{k} = -c\)), retains its polarization along the \(x\)-axis, and has the opposite sign relative to the incident electric field. Thus, the reflected wave is \(\mathbf{E}_r = -E_0\hat{\mathbf{i}}\cos(kz + \omega t)\).

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q03 - Total momentum delivered to non-reflecting surface

questiontext.text: 8.3 Light with an energy flux of \(20\text{ W/cm}^2\) falls on a non-reflecting surface at normal incidence. If the surface has an area of \(30\text{ cm}^2\), the total momentum delivered (for complete absorption) during \(30\text{ minutes}\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Energy flux (intensity) \(I = 20\text{ W/cm}^2\), surface area \(A = 30\text{ cm}^2\), time duration \(t = 30\text{ minutes} = 30 \times 60\text{ s} = 1800\text{ s}\), and speed of light in vacuum \(c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\). The surface is non-reflecting (complete absorption) at normal incidence.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All incident electromagnetic energy is absorbed by the surface, so the final momentum of the absorbed radiation is zero and the momentum transferred to the surface equals the total incident momentum.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The total energy \(U\) incident on area \(A\) in time \(t\) is: \[U = I \cdot A \cdot t\] For complete absorption, the total momentum \(p\) delivered to the surface is: \[p = \frac{U}{c}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
First, compute the power incident on the surface: \[P = I \cdot A = \left(20\text{ W/cm}^2\right) \times \left(30\text{ cm}^2\right) = 600\text{ W}\] Next, compute the total energy absorbed in \(1800\text{ s}\): \[U = P \cdot t = 600\text{ J/s} \times 1800\text{ s} = 1.08 \times 10^6\text{ J}\] Now, compute the total momentum delivered: \[p = \frac{U}{c} = \frac{1.08 \times 10^6\text{ J}}{3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}} = 0.36 \times 10^{-2}\text{ kg m/s} = 36 \times 10^{-4}\text{ kg m/s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking units: \(\text{J}/(\text{m/s}) = (\text{kg m}^2/\text{s}^2)/(\text{m/s}) = \text{kg m/s}\), which is the SI unit of momentum. Therefore, the total momentum delivered is \(36 \times 10^{-4}\text{ kg m/s}\).

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q04 - Electric field intensity from 50 W bulb

questiontext.text: 8.4 The electric field intensity produced by the radiations coming from \(100\text{ W}\) bulb at a \(3\text{ m}\) distance is \(E\). The electric field intensity produced by the radiations coming from \(50\text{ W}\) bulb at the same distance is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Power of the first bulb \(P_1 = 100\text{ W}\), electric field intensity at distance \(r = 3\text{ m}\) is \(E_1 = E\). Power of the second bulb \(P_2 = 50\text{ W}\) at the same distance \(r = 3\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both bulbs radiate isotropically as point sources, and the same fraction of power is converted into electromagnetic radiation at the same distance \(r\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The intensity \(I\) of an electromagnetic wave at distance \(r\) from an isotropic source of power \(P\) is: \[I = \frac{P}{4\pi r^2}\] Also, the intensity of an electromagnetic wave is proportional to the square of the electric field intensity: \[I = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 c E_0^2 \propto E^2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
At a fixed distance \(r\), \(I \propto P\) and \(I \propto E^2\), which gives: \[E^2 \propto P \implies \frac{E_2}{E_1} = \sqrt{\frac{P_2}{P_1}}\] Substituting \(P_1 = 100\text{ W}\), \(P_2 = 50\text{ W}\), and \(E_1 = E\): \[\frac{E_2}{E} = \sqrt{\frac{50}{100}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \implies E_2 = \frac{E}{\sqrt{2}}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Halving the radiated power halves the intensity, which reduces the electric field amplitude by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\). Thus, the electric field intensity is \(\frac{E}{\sqrt{2}}\).

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q05 - Direction of propagation of electromagnetic wave

questiontext.text: 8.5 If \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) represent electric and magnetic field vectors of the electromagnetic wave, the direction of propagation of electromagnetic wave is along

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An electromagnetic wave is a transverse wave in which the electric field vector \(\mathbf{E}\), the magnetic field vector \(\mathbf{B}\), and the direction of wave propagation are mutually perpendicular.

Step 2: Evaluation
The direction of energy transport and wave propagation is given by the Poynting vector: \[\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B})\]

Step 3: Application
By the right-hand rule for the cross product \(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\), curling the fingers from \(\mathbf{E}\) toward \(\mathbf{B}\) causes the thumb to point in the direction of wave propagation.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the direction of propagation of the electromagnetic wave is along \(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\).

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q06 - Ratio of electric and magnetic field intensity contributions

questiontext.text: 8.6 The ratio of contributions made by the electric field and magnetic field components to the intensity of an EM wave is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We consider a plane electromagnetic wave propagating in vacuum with electric field amplitude \(E_0\) and magnetic field amplitude \(B_0\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In vacuum, the electric and magnetic field amplitudes are related by \(E_0 = cB_0\), and the speed of light is \(c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The intensity of an EM wave is proportional to the average energy density \(u_{\text{avg}} = u_E + u_B\), where: \[u_E = \frac{1}{4}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2 \quad \text{and} \quad u_B = \frac{B_0^2}{4\mu_0}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute \(B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c}\) and \(c^2 = \frac{1}{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\) into \(u_B\): \[u_B = \frac{(E_0/c)^2}{4\mu_0} = \frac{E_0^2}{4\mu_0 c^2} = \frac{E_0^2}{4\mu_0 \left(\frac{1}{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\right)} = \frac{1}{4}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2 = u_E\] Therefore, the ratio of their contributions to intensity is: \[\frac{I_E}{I_B} = \frac{u_E}{u_B} = \frac{1}{1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
In an electromagnetic wave, the total energy is shared equally between the electric and magnetic fields. Thus, the ratio of their contributions to the intensity is \(1 : 1\).

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQI_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q07 - Fall-off of electric field from dipole antenna

questiontext.text: 8.7 An EM wave radiates outwards from a dipole antenna, with \(E_0\) as the amplitude of its electric field vector. The electric field \(E_0\) which transports significant energy from the source falls off as

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the radiation zone (far field) of an oscillating dipole antenna, electromagnetic energy spreads out over spherical wavefronts of surface area \(4\pi r^2\).

Step 2: Evaluation
By conservation of energy, the intensity \(I\) (power per unit area) falls off with distance \(r\) as: \[I \propto \frac{1}{r^2}\]

Step 3: Application
Since the intensity of an electromagnetic wave is proportional to the square of the electric field amplitude (\(I \propto E_0^2\)), we have: \[E_0^2 \propto \frac{1}{r^2} \implies E_0 \propto \frac{1}{r}\] (Near-field terms proportional to \(\frac{1}{r^2}\) and \(\frac{1}{r^3}\) decay much faster and do not transport significant energy to large distances.)

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the electric field amplitude \(E_0\) that transports significant energy from the source falls off as \(\frac{1}{r}\).

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQII_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q08 - Associated magnetic field and polarization of EM wave

questiontext.text: 8.8 An electromagnetic wave travels in vacuum along \(z\) direction: \(\mathbf{E} = (E_1\hat{\mathbf{i}} + E_2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\cos(kz - \omega t)\). Choose the correct options from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An electromagnetic wave propagates in vacuum along the \(+z\)-direction (unit propagation vector \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\)) with electric field \(\mathbf{E} = (E_1\hat{\mathbf{i}} + E_2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\cos(kz - \omega t)\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(E_1\) and \(E_2\) are constant real amplitudes, and the \(x\)- and \(y\)-components oscillate in phase with the same cosine factor \(\cos(kz - \omega t)\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a plane EM wave in vacuum propagating along \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\), the associated magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) is given by: \[\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{c}(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \mathbf{E})\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Computing the cross product using \(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \hat{\mathbf{i}} = \hat{\mathbf{j}}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \hat{\mathbf{j}} = -\hat{\mathbf{i}}\): \[\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{c}\left[\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times (E_1\hat{\mathbf{i}} + E_2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\right]\cos(kz - \omega t) = \frac{1}{c}(E_1\hat{\mathbf{j}} - E_2\hat{\mathbf{i}})\cos(kz - \omega t)\] Furthermore, because both components of \(\mathbf{E}\) oscillate in phase, the direction of \(\mathbf{E}\) remains fixed along the constant vector \((E_1\hat{\mathbf{i}} + E_2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\) in the \(xy\)-plane. Hence, the wave is plane (linearly) polarised, not circularly polarised.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking orthogonality: \(\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B} \propto (E_1\hat{\mathbf{i}} + E_2\hat{\mathbf{j}}) \cdot (-E_2\hat{\mathbf{i}} + E_1\hat{\mathbf{j}}) = -E_1 E_2 + E_2 E_1 = 0\), confirming \(\mathbf{E} \perp \mathbf{B}\). Thus, the associated magnetic field is \(\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{c}(E_1\hat{\mathbf{j}} - E_2\hat{\mathbf{i}})\cos(kz - \omega t)\) and the given electromagnetic wave is plane polarised.

answer.text: The associated magnetic field is given as \(\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{c}(E_1\hat{\mathbf{i}} - E_2\hat{\mathbf{j}})\cos(kz - \omega t)\).
The associated magnetic field is given as \(\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{c}(E_1\hat{\mathbf{j}} - E_2\hat{\mathbf{i}})\cos(kz - \omega t)\).
The given electromagnetic field is circularly polarised.
The given electromagnetic wave is plane polarised.

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQII_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q09 - Vector relations for EM wave along z-axis

questiontext.text: 8.9 An electromagnetic wave travelling along \(z\)-axis is given as: \(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{E}_0\cos(kz - \omega t)\). Choose the correct options from the following:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A plane electromagnetic wave propagates along the \(+z\)-axis (unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\)) with electric field \(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{E}_0\cos(kz - \omega t)\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The wave is a transverse electromagnetic wave in vacuum with \(\omega = ck\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a transverse EM wave propagating along \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\):
1. \(\mathbf{E}\), \(\mathbf{B}\), and \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\) are mutually perpendicular: \(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\).
2. \(\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{c}(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \mathbf{E}) = \frac{k}{\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \mathbf{E})\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- Since \(\frac{1}{c} = \frac{k}{\omega} \neq \frac{1}{\omega}\) in general, writing \(\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \mathbf{E})\) is dimensionally incorrect.
- Taking the cross product of \(\mathbf{B}\) with \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\): \[c(\mathbf{B} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}}) = (\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \mathbf{E}) \times \hat{\mathbf{k}} = \mathbf{E}(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{k}}) - \hat{\mathbf{k}}(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \mathbf{E}) = \mathbf{E}(1) - 0 = \mathbf{E}\] Thus, \(\mathbf{E} = c(\mathbf{B} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}})\) is valid.
- Because \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are both perpendicular to the propagation direction \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\), their dot products with \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\) vanish: \(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\) (whereas their cross products with \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\) are non-zero).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, the valid relations are \(\mathbf{E} = c(\mathbf{B} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}})\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \mathbf{E} = 0, \hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\).

answer.text: The associated magnetic field is given as \(\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{c}\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \mathbf{E} = \frac{1}{\omega}(\hat{\mathbf{k}} \times \mathbf{E})\)
The electromagnetic field can be written in terms of the associated magnetic field as \(\mathbf{E} = c(\mathbf{B} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}})\).

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQII_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q10 - Valid E and B pairs for x-propagating wave

questiontext.text: 8.10 A plane electromagnetic wave propagating along \(x\) direction can have the following pairs of \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a plane electromagnetic wave, the electric field vector \(\mathbf{E}\) and magnetic field vector \(\mathbf{B}\) are mutually perpendicular, and both are perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Since the wave propagates along the \(x\)-direction, neither \(\mathbf{E}\) nor \(\mathbf{B}\) can have a component along the \(x\)-axis (\(E_x = 0\) and \(B_x = 0\)).

Step 3: Application
Therefore, \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) must lie in the \(yz\)-plane and be perpendicular to each other. This allows the pairs \((E_y, B_z)\) and \((E_z, B_y)\), while any pair containing \(E_x\) or \(B_x\) is invalid.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Thus, the valid pairs of \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are \(E_y, B_z\) and \(E_z, B_y\).

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQII_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q11 - Electromagnetic waves from oscillating charged particle

questiontext.text: 8.11 A charged particle oscillates about its mean equilibrium position with a frequency of \(10^9\text{ Hz}\). The electromagnetic waves produced:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Frequency of oscillation of the charged particle is \( u = 10^9 ext{ Hz}\). Speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum is \(c = 3 imes 10^8 ext{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The electromagnetic wave produced by an oscillating charge in free space propagates at speed \(c\) with the same frequency as the source oscillation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Frequency of the emitted EM wave equals the oscillation frequency of the charge: \( u_{ ext{wave}} = u\).
2. Wavelength is given by: \[\lambda = rac{c}{ u}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- The frequency of the produced electromagnetic waves is \( u = 10^9 ext{ Hz}\).
- Calculating the wavelength: \[\lambda = rac{3 imes 10^8 ext{ m/s}}{10^9 ext{ Hz}} = 0.3 ext{ m}\] - A frequency of \(10^9 ext{ Hz}\) (and wavelength \(0.3 ext{ m}\)) lies in the radiowaves region of the electromagnetic spectrum.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking \(c = u\lambda = 10^9 imes 0.3 = 3 imes 10^8 ext{ m/s}\). Thus, the electromagnetic waves produced will have a frequency of \(10^9 ext{ Hz}\), will have a wavelength of \(0.3 ext{ m}\), and fall in the region of radiowaves.

questiontext.text: 8.12 The source of electromagnetic waves can be a charge

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Maxwell's electromagnetic theory, an accelerating electric charge radiates electromagnetic waves, whereas a stationary charge or a charge moving with constant velocity does not radiate.

Step 2: Evaluation
- A charge at rest has zero acceleration and produces only a static electric field.
- A charge moving with a constant velocity has zero acceleration and produces steady electric and magnetic fields without radiation.
- A charge moving in a circular orbit experiences continuous centripetal acceleration due to the changing direction of its velocity.
- A charge falling in an electric field experiences a net electrostatic force \(q\mathbf{E}\) and therefore accelerates.

Step 3: Application
Only the states involving non-zero acceleration act as sources of electromagnetic waves.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the source of electromagnetic waves can be a charge moving in a circular orbit or a charge falling in an electric field.

name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_MCQII_ELECTROMAGNETICWAVES_MCQ_Q13 - Radiation pressure on surfaces in vacuum

questiontext.text: 8.13 An EM wave of intensity \(I\) falls on a surface kept in vacuum and exerts radiation pressure \(p\) on it. Which of the following are true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An electromagnetic wave of intensity \(I\) falls normally on a surface in vacuum, exerting radiation pressure \(p\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Intensity \(I\) is the energy incident per unit area per unit time, so the incident momentum per unit area per unit time is \(\frac{I}{c}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Radiation pressure equals the rate of change of momentum per unit area: \[p = \frac{\Delta p_{\text{surf}}}{A \Delta t}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
- For a totally absorbing surface, the reflected momentum is zero, so the momentum transferred per unit area per unit time is: \[p = \frac{I}{c} - 0 = \frac{I}{c}\] - For a totally reflecting surface, the wave's momentum reverses direction, so the change in momentum per unit area per unit time is: \[p = \frac{I}{c} - \left(-\frac{I}{c}\right) = \frac{2I}{c}\] - For real surfaces, partial absorption and partial reflection occur (reflectance \(0 < R < 1\)), so the radiation pressure lies strictly between the two extremes: \[\frac{I}{c} < p < \frac{2I}{c}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, the radiation pressure is \(\frac{I}{c}\) for total absorption, \(\frac{2I}{c}\) for total reflection, and in the range \(\frac{I}{c} < p < \frac{2I}{c}\) for real surfaces.

answer.text: Radiation pressure is \(I / c\) if the wave is totally absorbed.
Radiation pressure is \(I / c\) if the wave is totally reflected.
Radiation pressure is \(2I / c\) if the wave is totally reflected.
Radiation pressure is in the range \(I / c < p < 2I / c\) for real surfaces.
